Bach · Well-Tempered Clavier I · Fugue 21 of 24

Fugue in B♭ Major, BWV 866 Three-Voice Dance

A cheerful three-voice fugue in 3/4 with a subject that leaps through the tonic chord and then runs in sixteenths. It has the easy swing of a minuet.

  • 48 bars, 3/4
  • 3 voices
  • 5 entries found
  • 0 in stretto
  • 4 episodes
  • answer tonal

Answer

Tonal

  • RWhere the subject moves between ① and ⑤ near its start, the answer exchanges them (⑤ answers ①, ① answers ⑤) so the music stays near the home key: Marpurg’s tonal answer (Mann pp. 166–169).
  • FBach’s answer is tonal: it starts F against the subject’s F, and the interval after note are adjusted; after that it is a plain transposition.
  • FOrder of entry in the exposition: soprano (subject), bass (subject), alto (subject).
Countersubject

Free Counterpoint

  • FNo regular countersubject was found: the line against the answer does not come back with later entries. ours
  • RMarpurg: a counterpart should differ from the theme in rhythm and motion (Mann pp. 199–201).

No Stretto

The Six Steps

Scott Roberts’s method (2004) asks what is notable in the opening and whether the fugue later answers it. Roberts does not analyze this fugue, and the findings below come from the automatic analysis, so all of them are ours.

  1. STEP 1

    Identify the Traditional Fugue Elements

    Mark every entry, the countersubject, codettas, episodes and coda.

    • 5 entries (5 complete).
    • 0 regular countersubjects; 4 episodes; a coda.
  2. STEP 2

    Find the Notable Properties

    Look in the exposition for linear lines (complete or blocked), patterns, suspended degrees and contrasts.

    • A falling line: the subject’s longest stepwise run is ① ⑦ ⑥ ⑤ (4 notes).
    • Top note: ② (C); the whole fugue reaches C at m. 17, beat 3.
  3. STEPS 3–5

    Patterns and Other Segmentations

    Look for growing, shrinking or mirrored section lengths, and for other ways to cut the fugue.

    Section lengths in bars: 2 + 6 + 2 + 11 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 9 + 2 + 9.8. The cadences found cut it at m. 48.

  4. STEP 6

    Decide How the Fugue Responds

    A property is reconciled when it comes back with the trait that made it notable, now completed.

    Not answered by this test. No line in the last bars carries the subject’s falling line further. That points to a literal fugue in Roberts’s terms; the reading is ours.

Articulation: HIP and Busoni

Bach wrote no dots or dynamics in this fugue, and no slurs. The score above can show two answers to that silence: a reading built from eighteenth-century treatises, and Busoni’s marks of 1894. Switch between them with the Articulation control on the score; playback follows the layer you pick.

  • Staccato: a little less than half the value
  • Tenuto: full value
  • Dash and dot: weighted but separated
  • Slur: full value, slight weight on the first note
  • Comma: lift before an entry

The HIP Reading ours

The rules are the treatises’ own. Deciding which notes they apply to is our reading, made by the same rules for every fugue in the book. Outside the subject, every stepwise group of three or more short notes within one beat (one bar in 3/8 and 6/16), in any voice, gets a slur as well.

  • RUnmarked quarters and eighths in a moderate tempo get the ordinary touch: about half their value, played with some fire (C. P. E. Bach III §22, p. 157). No sign is written for it, so these notes stay unmarked.
  • RDetached notes belong mostly to leaps and quicker tempos and last a little less than half their value (III §17, p. 154). Quantz gives leaping eighths the short tongue stroke (VI, p. 73).
  • RSlurred notes are held full length and belong mostly to stepwise motion; the first note under a slur gets a slight pressure (III §18, pp. 154–155).
  • RA note marked Ten., a tied note and the dot of a dotted note are held (III §22, p. 157; §23, pp. 157–158; §25, p. 159).
  • RIn runs every note is distinct, yet the fingers are not lifted early: Quantz describes drawing the fingertips back along the keys as J. S. Bach’s own manner (XVII.vi §18, pp. 259–260).
  • RGive more weight to the note on which a subject enters, to long notes among quick ones and to dissonances (Quantz XVII.vi §10–11, pp. 253–254; C. P. E. Bach III §29, p. 163).
  • RBreathe before a returning subject and take the time from the note before (Quantz VII, pp. 87–88). GAt the keyboard this becomes a small lift before each entry. ours

Busoni’s Marks Busoni

  • FTempo: Allegretto semplice.
  • FOpening: mf.
  • FSubject: A slur over the opening leaps ending on a short note.
  • FThe scan used here is a library copy with an earlier owner’s pencil marks; only Busoni’s printed marks are used.
  • FThe subject is marked the same way at each entry; the last bars are “risoluto” and ff, and he prints Hoffmeister’s easier version of the ending as an alternative.
  • FHe notes that the fugue uses only the subject and its two countersubjects, and that its “development” is simply the three of them inverted against each other.
  • FHe calls it easygoing throughout, without intellectual depth but never shallow, smooth and rounded in form. (The scan used here has a former owner’s pencil notes, which are ignored.)
  • ours His marks were read entry by entry from his edition. Where he repeats the first statement’s slurs and dots, the score repeats them on that entry; the table below lists what he prints on each one.

How Playback Reads the Marks

Each layer changes only how long a note sounds, as a share of its written value. HIP: staccato 42%, unmarked eighths 55%, the last note of a slur 80%, quarters 70%, sixteenths 92%, slurred, dotted, tied and long notes 95–100%, the note before an entry 60%. Busoni: legato, 97%; his staccato 45%, dash and dot 65%. Dynamics and tempo changes are not played. These numbers are ours.

Urtext and Busoni

The Urtext NBA

The Bärenreiter urtext (Neue Bach-Ausgabe, ed. Alfred Dürr) gives the fugue without tempo or dynamics or slurs. The encoding used here has 0 ornament signs.

Busoni’s Edition Busoni

  • Adds a tempo (Allegretto semplice), dynamics, articulation and fingering.

About This Score

Notes and Layout

The score is engraved from David Huron’s Humdrum encoding of the Bach-Gesellschaft edition (BG 14, 1866). Unlike the C major and C minor pages, the notes were not compared note by note with a second edition.

Each voice has its own staff (open score). Bach’s keyboard layout puts two voices on each staff. Line breaks are the engraver’s.

Playback uses recorded samples: the Steinway Grand by default, or an Italian harpsichord at A = 415.

What Comes From Where

  • R Rules are precepts of a named theorist, here Marpurg and Fux as given in Mann’s Study of Fugue, cited by page.
  • Busoni Tempo, and his marks on every entry of the subject and countersubject.
  • ours Everything else was found by a program that matches the subject’s rhythm and shape in every voice, then reads keys, stretto, countersubjects, cadences (⑤–① in the bass under a leading tone, on a strong beat), sequences and pedals from the notes. It can miss entries whose rhythm Bach changes, and it does not name harmonies. Treat the tables as a careful first reading, not a final one.
